history.ask: Pain on swallowing (odynophagia) or chest pain

red_flags: Progressive dysphagia with weight loss at age over 40 — esophageal carcinoma until proven otherwise; urgent surgical referral
Complete obstruction — unable to swallow even saliva
Dysphagia with anemia or overt GI bleeding
Hoarseness accompanying dysphagia — recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement
Recurrent aspiration pneumonia — the swallow is unsafe
exam: Weigh the patient and assess muscle wasting and hydration
Watch the patient swallow a sip of water — coughing, wet voice, or repeated attempts localize an oropharyngeal problem
Palpate the neck for a goiter and check whether it moves on swallowing
Feel for a soft gurgling neck swelling that empties on pressure — pharyngeal pouch
Palpate the supraclavicular fossae — a hard left node (Virchow) supports advanced carcinoma
Inspect the mouth, tongue, and pharynx — glossitis and angular stomatitis support iron deficiency
Inspect nails for koilonychia and conjunctiva for pallor
Auscultate the chest — basal crackles of aspiration
Palpate the epigastrium for a mass and the liver for irregular enlargement
Assess the voice — hoarseness alongside the swallowing complaint

investigations.why: Iron-deficiency anemia supports esophageal web (Plummer-Vinson) or a bleeding carcinoma; normal blood count fits achalasia, spasm, and globus
Confirms the iron deficiency behind a suspected web and grades the anemia of malignancy

First-line and widely available: bird-beak taper rules in achalasia, an irregular shouldered stricture points to carcinoma, a smooth taper to peptic stricture, a posterior pouch to Zenker's — and it is the safer first test when a pouch is suspected before any scope

Widened mediastinum or an air-fluid level behind the heart supports megaesophagus of achalasia; aspiration changes support an unsafe swallow; a retrosternal goiter shadow supports extrinsic compression

investigations.test: TSH + thyroid ultrasound (if neck swelling found)
investigations.why: Characterizes a goiter causing extrinsic compression and its functional status

Second-line in sequence but OBLIGATORY — regardless of what barium shows — if any alarm feature is present: progressive dysphagia over 40, weight loss, anemia or GI bleeding, or any stricture, mass, or mucosal lesion on barium. Biopsy is the only way to prove or exclude carcinoma and to separate peptic from malignant stricture; a 'benign-looking' barium never closes the question
Second-line — if endoscopy and barium are non-diagnostic and a motility disorder is suspected: confirms achalasia and diffuse spasm
